t: African Americans and their allies fought the segregation and disenfranchisement imposed on the South after Reconstruction with lawsuits, boycotts, sit-ins, freedom rides, marches and voter drives.
Non-violent campaigns from Montgomery to Selma met violent resistance, and the images of that violence helped persuade Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
From 1965 the movement divided over Black Power, northern poverty and the Vietnam War, and the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. in 1968 is often taken as the end of its classic phase.
dyk: Rosa Parks was not the first to refuse: in March 1955, nine months before her arrest, the fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin was arrested for keeping her seat on a Montgomery bus, and she was a plaintiff in the case that desegregated them.
ev: The Supreme Court rules segregated public schools unconstitutional in Brown v. Board of Education
Rosa Parks’s arrest starts the Montgomery bus boycott, led by Martin Luther King Jr.
Federal troops escort nine Black students into Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas
Student sit-ins spread across the South, and Freedom Riders challenge segregated bus travel
The Birmingham campaign and the March on Washington, where King speaks of his dream
The Civil Rights Act outlaws segregation in public places and discrimination in employment
The Selma to Montgomery marches lead to the Voting Rights Act
Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated in Memphis, and Congress passes the Fair Housing Act

f.where: The southern United States, above all Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, Tennessee and the Carolinas, with campaigns in Washington, D.C., and in northern cities such as Chicago
f.period: 1954–1968: from the Supreme Court’s ruling in Brown v. Board of Education to the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. and the Fair Housing Act; its roots reach back to the 1930s and 1940s
f.figures: Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, Thurgood Marshall, Ella Baker, John Lewis, Fannie Lou Hamer
f.outcome: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 ended legal segregation and most barriers to Black voting in the South, though economic inequality and segregation in practice persisted
